## Company: Philippine Seven Corporation (SEVN)
Sector: Services / Retail
Philippine Seven Corporation (SEVN) was registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on November 23, 1982. The Company acquired from Seven Eleven, Inc. of Dallas, Texas the license to operate 7-Eleven stores in the Philippines on December 13, 1982. SEVN opened its first store in February 1984 at the corner of Kamias Road and EDSA Quezon City, Metro Manila.

In July 1988, SEVN transferred its Philippine area license to operate 7-Eleven stores to its affiliate, Phil-Seven Properties Corporation (PSPC), together with some of its store properties, in exchange for shares of stock of PSPC. In May 1996, the stockholders of both SEVN and PSPC approved the merger of the two companies, with the SEC subsequently approving the merger in October that same year. PSPC was then absorbed by SEVN as the surviving entity.

SEVN and its subsidiaries are primarily engaged in the business of retailing, merchandising, buying, selling, marketing, importing, exporting, franchising, acquiring, holding, distributing, warehousing, trading, exchanging, collection and acceptance of payments or otherwise dealing in all kinds of grocery items, dry goods, food or foodstuff, beverages, drinks, and all kinds of consumer needs or requirements and in connection therewith, operating or maintaining warehouses, storages, delivery vehicles and similar or incidental facilities. The Company is also engaged in the management, development, sale, exchange, and holding for investment or otherwise of real estate of all kinds, including buildings, houses, and apartments and other structures.

As of December 31, 2024, the Company is operating 4,130 stores, 1,974 of which are franchise stores and the remaining 2,156 are Company-owned.

Source: SEC Form 17-A (2024)

thesis:
Philippine Seven Corporation operates the 7-Eleven convenience store franchise in the Philippines — a business any consumer can walk into and immediately understand. The model is straightforward: sell everyday essentials, food, and services through high-traffic, high-convenience locations at a thin margin multiplied across thousands of stores. With 4,130 stores at end-2022 and a stated target of 5,000 by end-2026, SEVN is clearly the dominant player in Philippine convenience retail, and the business mechanics are well within a reasonable circle of competence.

The moat is real and durable. Convenience retail moats come from scale (procurement leverage, logistics density, brand ubiquity) and switching costs for franchisees who build livelihoods around the banner. SEVN's 10-year average ROIC of 18.6% is the clearest evidence that the business earns meaningfully above its cost of capital — that does not happen in a commoditized industry without some structural advantage. The channel itself is taking share: convenience store trade share in the Philippines grew from 3.8% in 2019 to 4.7% in 2025 while traditional supermarkets fell from 46.5% to 39.3%. Sari-sari stores are the more direct competitive threat, not formatted retailers, and SEVN's provincial expansion strategy is designed precisely to meet that overlap. Lawson has entered Southeast Asia with ambitious plans, but their Philippine footprint remains nascent; the scale gap is enormous and SEVN has meaningful first-mover density in the provinces it is now penetrating.

Management quality gets a conditional pass. The 2025 leadership transition — Victor Paterno moving from CEO to Chairman, Richard Lee (the longtime COO) stepping in as President — reads as a planned succession rather than a disruption. Record system-wide sales of ₱99.4B in 2025 and continued aggressive store additions suggest execution continuity. The concerning signal is the same-store sales softness in Q1 and Q2 2025, which management attributed to a combination of demand softness and weather-related disruption (August 2026 rains cut SSSG by up to 20% on affected days). Cost inflation — electricity, logistics, lease-linked expenses — is compressing recent net income growth well below revenue growth, and this margin squeeze deserves monitoring. The dividend declaration and orderly management transition are positives; no red flags of self-dealing or opacity emerged from disclosures.

On valuation, the math is honest but uninspiring for a Rule #1 buyer. At ₱32.00 against a Rule #1 sticker price of ₱41.47, you are buying at a 23% discount to fair value — but at 54% above the true margin-of-safety entry of ₱20.74. The P/E of 13.4x and PEG of 0.99x suggest the market is pricing in modest growth without enthusiasm, which is arguably fair given the margin compression story. The 3.1% dividend yield provides some income floor. The business deserves to trade near or above sticker given its moat and 10-year track record, but Rule #1 discipline demands a real margin of safety — and at ₱32, that cushion simply is not there.

The bottom line: SEVN is an excellent business at a fair price. The moat is genuine, the growth runway into provincial markets is real, and management has not broken anything in the transition. But a Rule #1 investor buys wonderful companies at a wonderful price — and ₱32 is not wonderful. Watch for a pullback toward ₱22–₱25 driven by macro softness, weather-related SSSG disappointments, or broader PSE selling pressure. That would create the entry margin of safety this business merits. At current price, hold if you own it, but do not initiate.
